content: 1. A study published in HIV Medicine in 2012 examined the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and associated risk compensation behaviors among men who have sex with men (MSM) accessing genitourinary (GU) services. 2. Holt et al. (2013) explored the attitudes of HIV-negative and HIV-positive gay men toward antiretroviral-based prevention methods, including PrEP, as well as their perspectives on HIV treatments and other medicines. This study was published in AIDS Behavior. 3. Another study by Holt et al. (2012) investigated the willingness of Australian gay and bisexual men to use PrEP and the potential for decreased condom use. The study found that these factors were associated with unprotected anal intercourse and the perceived likelihood of acquiring HIV. This research was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 4. A systematic review conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2014 aimed to inform consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations, including MSM, with a focus on PrEP. 5. Van der Elst et al. (2013) reported high acceptability of PrEP among at-risk populations in Kenya, but adherence and consistent use posed significant challenges. This qualitative study was based on a Phase I trial of both intermittent and daily PrEP regimens and was published in AIDS Behavior. 6. A survey conducted by Ndegwa et al. (2013) assessed community opinions and preferences regarding PrEP, microbicides, and vaccines across five regions in Kenya, focusing on key populations. The findings were presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. 7. Leonardi, Lee, and Tan (2011) examined awareness, usage, and willingness to use PrEP among men in downtown Toronto, Canada. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 8. Krznaric and Knecht (2013) investigated attitudes toward PrEP among MSM in Germany. Their findings were presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. 9. Krakower et al. (2012) explored anticipated risk compensation behaviors associated with PrEP use among North American MSM using an internet-based social network. This study was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 10. Mimiaga and Mayer (2013) found that MSM in Latin America, Spain, and Portugal who used internet social networking sites had limited awareness of PrEP but expressed high interest in its use for preventing sexual acquisition of HIV. These findings were presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention. 11. Eisingerich et al. (2012) conducted a multinational study to assess attitudes and acceptance of oral and injectable PrEP among potential user groups. The results were published in PLoS One. 12. Arreola and Ayala (2012) examined social and structural barriers and facilitators to accessing PrEP, HIV testing, and treatment among gay and other MSM in the Global South and Global North. Their findings were presented at the 19th International AIDS Conference in Washington, DC. 13. Wilson and colleagues (2012) identified predictors of knowledge and interest in PrEP and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) use among MSM through a global, multilingual survey. These findings were presented at the 19th International AIDS Conference. 14. Tellalian et al. (2013) surveyed HIV healthcare providers to evaluate their knowledge, attitudes, and prescribing practices regarding PrEP. The results were published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs. 15. Karris et al. (2013) assessed the opinions of healthcare providers in the United States and Canada on the real-world use of PrEP. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 16. Kapur et al. (2012) investigated the knowledge, attitudes, and willingness of New York City healthcare providers to prescribe oral PrEP for HIV prevention. These findings were presented at the 19th International AIDS Conference. 17. Arnold et al. (2012) conducted a qualitative study to explore provider perspectives on implementing PrEP in clinical settings to prevent HIV infection. The study was published in PLoS One. 18. Calabrese et al. (2013) examined the impact of patient race on clinical decisions related to prescribing PrEP, focusing on assumptions about sexual risk compensation and implications for access. This study was published in AIDS Behavior. 19. Tang et al. (2013) explored provider attitudes toward oral PrEP for HIV prevention among high-risk MSM in Lima, Peru. The findings were published in AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses. 20. Taegtmeyer et al. (2013) highlighted the challenges of providing counseling to MSM in highly stigmatized contexts in Kenya. This qualitative study was published in PLoS One.
